title: Wesley on horseback
hookLine: a clergyman who loved order takes to the saddle and preaches in fields to working people

cards: John Wesley likes things done properly. He's a Church of England clergyman, trained at Oxford, and he believes preaching belongs in a church, from a pulpit, in good order.
He later admits he'd been so attached to decency and order that saving souls outside a church would once have seemed to him almost a sin. But churches are closing their pulpits to him.

To some clergy, his preaching is too warm, too urgent. Meanwhile, outside the city, there are working people, coal miners among them, who seldom if ever set foot in a parish church. So Wesley has a choice.

teach.b: He goes outside. His journal records the day he first preached in the open air, and the phrase is startling: he "submitted to be more vile." He's borrowing from King David.
In Second Samuel, as the ark of God comes into Jerusalem, David dances before the LORD with all his might, and his wife Michal despises him for it. David answers, "I will yet be more vile than thus."
In other words: if worship makes me look undignified, so be it. So the man of order stands on a rise of ground in a field to preach. From then on, he travels.

On horseback, year after year, along muddy roads and through all weathers, to towns, villages, mining districts, marketplaces. Tradition says he read books in the saddle, letting the horse find the way.

teach.h: ALL THE WORLD AS MY PARISH.
teach.b: When church officials objected that he was preaching in other men's parishes, he answered with a line from his journal: "I look upon all the world as my parish."
Wherever he was, he felt bound to share the good news with anyone willing to hear. He didn't gather them into a new church at first.
Wesley stayed a Church of England clergyman and urged his hearers to go to their parish churches.
He organized them into small groups, societies and classes, to meet and pray between Sundays, and those groups became the Methodist movement.

teach.h: OUT TO THE HIGHWAYS AND HEDGES.
teach.b: Jesus tells a parable about a feast where the invited guests won't come, so the host sends his servant out, in the King James words, "into the highways and hedges." Wesley took the road literally.

how: Methodist churches grew from Wesley's societies and classes, and Christians in different churches still take worship outdoors, to street corners, parks and workplaces, to meet people who don't come inside.

games.q: you're John Wesley. pulpits are closing to you, and the people you most want to reach seldom come to church. what do you do?
o: wait for the pulpits to open again.
go outside and preach where they are.
write a book and hope they read it.
games.why: he submitted to be more vile, preached in the open air, and spent years on horseback: all the world as his parish.

practice: Bring to mind one person who won't come to you: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker, an old friend. Picture where they actually are today, their kitchen, their shift, their bench in the park, and hold them there as you breathe.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wonder what it would take to go to them instead of waiting.
